ai.literal: Do not desire, even if you win, gambling; even that which is won is like a fish swallowing the hook.
ai.translation: Do not desire to gamble even if you win; for even what you win is like a fish swallowing the baited hook.
ai.modern: வெற்றி பெற்றாலும் சூதாட்டத்தை விரும்பக் கூடாது; அதில் வென்ற பொருளும், தூண்டில் முள்ளை மீன் விழுங்குவதைப் போன்றதே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the temptation of gambling, even when one is winning. The poet compares the winnings of gambling to the attractive bait on a fishhook. Just as a fish eagerly swallows the bait only to be trapped and killed by the hidden hook, a gambler is lured by initial gains only to face ultimate ruin. Thus, the apparent gain in gambling is merely a trap that leads to destruction.

ai.literal: Having obtained one, losing a hundred, even to gamblers, is there indeed a way of living having obtained goodness?
ai.translation: Can there ever be a way for gamblers, who gain but one thing only to lose a hundred, to attain prosperity and live a good life?
ai.modern: ஒன்றைப் பெற்று நூறை இழக்கின்ற சூதாடிகளுக்கு, நன்மையை அடைந்து வாழ்வதற்கு ஏதேனும் ஒரு வழி உண்டோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the futility and ruinous nature of gambling. The poet points out that a gambler might occasionally win a single gain ('ஒன்று'), but in the process, they inevitably lose a hundredfold ('நூறு'). Because of this disproportionate loss, the poet rhetorically asks if there can ever be a viable path ('ஆறு') for such gamblers to attain true prosperity ('நன்று') and lead a stable, good life. The contrast between gaining one and losing a hundred vividly illustrates how gambling leads to certain financial and moral bankruptcy.

ai.literal: If one speaks of the rolling dice gain without ceasing, the wealth gain will go outside and fall.
ai.translation: If a person constantly speaks of and plays the rolling dice game without ceasing, their accumulated wealth and income will depart and fall into the hands of others.
ai.modern: உருளும் பகடையின் லாபத்தைப் பற்றி இடைவிடாமல் பேசிக்கொண்டு (சூதாடிக்கொண்டு) இருந்தால், ஒருவனுடைய செல்வமும் வருவாயும் அவனை விட்டு நீங்கிப் பிறரிடம் போய்ச் சேரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the addictive nature of gambling. The poet contrasts 'உருளாயம்' (the gain from rolling dice) with 'பொருளாயம்' (the gain of real wealth and income). If a person is constantly obsessed with the rolling dice and speaks of it without ceasing ('ஓவாது கூறின்'), their actual earned wealth and income will vanish ('போஒய்') and end up in the hands of others ('புறமே படும்'). The word 'ஓவாது' highlights how the relentless, non-stop pursuit of gambling leads directly to financial ruin.

ai.literal: Misery many causing, prosperity destroying, than gambling, poverty bringing one thing is not.
ai.translation: There is nothing else that brings such utter poverty as gambling, which inflicts many miseries and ruins one's prosperity.
ai.modern: பல துன்பங்களை உண்டாக்கி, சிறப்பையும் செல்வத்தையும் அழிக்கும் சூதாட்டத்தைப் போல, வறுமையைத் தரும் வேறு ஒரு செயல் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the destructive nature of gambling. It explains that gambling inflicts multiple miseries (ciṟumai) upon a person and completely ruins their wealth and social standing (cīr). The poet emphasizes that there is absolutely no other vice or misfortune (oṉṟu il) that drags a person into such deep destitution (vaṟumai) as gambling does. The word 'cīr' is crucial here, representing both material prosperity and the honor or reputation that a person loses when they gamble.

ai.literal: And the dice, and the gambling den, and the hand, having exulted in, those who eagerly coveted, having become nothing, who?
ai.translation: Who among those who eagerly coveted and exulted in the dice, the gambling den, and their own hand's play, has not been reduced to absolute nothingness?
ai.modern: சூதாடும் கவறு, சூதாடும் இடம், தன் கைத்திறமை ஆகியவற்றைத் தற்பெருமையோடு விரும்பிச் சூதாடியவர்களுள், வறுமையடைந்து அழியாதவர் யார்?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the destructive nature of gambling by identifying its three core temptations: the dice, the gambling hall, and the player's belief in their own hand's skill. Those who pride themselves on these elements and eagerly pursue the game are destined for ruin. The word 'tarukki' suggests an arrogant obsession or self-confidence in one's luck or skill, while 'ivaṟiyār' points to the insatiable greed of the gambler. By asking 'who has not become nothing?' (illāki yār), the poet emphasizes that total destitution is the universal and inescapable outcome for all gamblers.

ai.literal: Their belly they will not fill, distress they will suffer, those who are enveloped by the goddess of misfortune called gambling.
ai.translation: Those who are enveloped by the goddess of misfortune called gambling will not even fill their bellies, and will suffer endless distress.
ai.modern: சூது என்று சொல்லப்படும் மூதேவியால் (வறுமைத் தெய்வத்தால்) மூடப்பட்டவர்கள், தம் வயிற்றைக்கூட நிரப்ப முடியாமல் துன்பத்தை அடைவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the devastating effects of gambling by personifying it as the goddess of misfortune. Those who fall into the trap of gambling are described as being completely enveloped or possessed by this destructive force. As a result, they lose everything, to the extent that they cannot even satisfy their basic hunger. Instead of wealth or pleasure, they are left to endure constant misery and distress.

ai.literal: If one enters spending time in the gambling den, it will destroy long-standing wealth and good character.
ai.translation: If a person enters a gambling den and wastes their time there, it will destroy both their inherited wealth and their good character.
ai.modern: சூதாடும் இடத்தில் தன் காலத்தைச் செலுத்தி நுழைந்தால், அது அவனுடைய பழைமையான செல்வத்தையும் நற்பண்பையும் அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the perils of entering a gambling den, referred to here as 'கழகம்'. The phrase 'காலை புகின்' points to the act of entering and wasting one's precious time in such places. The poet emphasizes that gambling does not merely cause financial ruin by wiping out long-standing, inherited wealth ('பழகிய செல்வம்'); it also degrades a person's moral character and innate goodness ('பண்பு'). Thus, the habit of gambling is doubly destructive, stripping a person of both material security and personal integrity.

ai.literal: Wealth having destroyed, falsehood having adopted, grace having destroyed, misery causing to suffer, gambling.
ai.translation: Gambling destroys one's wealth, drives them to adopt falsehood, ruins their compassion, and plunges them into endless misery.
ai.modern: சூதாட்டம் ஒருவனுடைய செல்வத்தை அழித்து, அவனைப் பொய் சொல்ல வைத்து, அவனுடைய இரக்க குணத்தையும் அழித்து, துன்பத்தில் உழலச் செய்யும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the destructive path of gambling on a person's life and character. First, it ruins their material wealth (poruḷ). To sustain the habit or cover losses, the gambler is forced to adopt falsehood (poy) and deceit. This moral decline eventually destroys their innate sense of grace and compassion (aruḷ) for others. Ultimately, the vice of gambling (cūtu) leaves the individual trapped in a state of perpetual suffering and misery (allal).

ai.literal: Clothing, wealth, food, reputation, and learning—these five will not reach a person if they take up gambling.
ai.translation: Clothing, wealth, food, reputation, and learning—these five things will never belong to those who take up gambling.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் சூதாட்டத்தை மேற்கொண்டால், அவனுக்கு ஆடை, செல்வம், உணவு, புகழ், கல்வி ஆகிய ஐந்துமே வந்து சேரமாட்டா.
ai.explanation: This couplet lists five essential elements of a dignified and prosperous life: clothing (decency), wealth (security), food (sustenance), reputation (honor), and learning (wisdom). The author warns that if a person yields to the vice of gambling, represented here by the word 'āyam', they will lose all five. The word 'oḷi' is used here in the sense of reputation or luster, which is quickly ruined by the shame of gambling. Ultimately, the habit of gambling strips a person of both their material needs and their intellectual and social standing.

ai.literal: As often as losing, desires, gambling-indeed like, suffering as often as, has love, the soul.
ai.translation: Just as a gambler loves play all the more as he loses, so does the soul love life all the more as it suffers pain.
ai.modern: சூதாட்டத்தில் இழக்க இழக்க மேலும் அதன் மேல் ஆசை கொள்ளும் சூதனைப் போல, துன்பங்களை அனுபவிக்க அனுபவிக்க இவ்வுயிர் உடலின் மேல் மேலும் பற்று வைக்கிறது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a striking analogy to describe the persistent nature of attachment. The word 'இழத்தொறூஉம்' (as often as one loses) is paired with 'உழத்தொறூஉம்' (as often as one suffers) to show parallel behaviors. Just as a gambler cannot walk away and desires the game even more with every loss, the soul ('உயிர்') develops an even stronger attachment ('காதற்று') to worldly life the more it undergoes suffering ('துன்பம்'). The poet highlights the irrationality of human attachment through the self-destructive obsession of gambling.
